name: Ruruuli-Lunyala
catalog_citation: Namyalo, Saudah, Alena Witzlack-Makarevich, Anatole Kiriggwajjo, Amos Atuhairwe, Zarina Molochieva, Ruth Mukama & Margaret Zellers. 2021. A dictionary and grammatical sketch of Ruruuli-Lunyala (African Language Grammars and Dictionaries 5). Berlin: Language S…
catalog_locator: ch. 2 Phonology and orthography, sec. 2.4 'A note on tone', p. 15 (also sec. 2.5 Syllable structure, pp. 15-16)
catalog_quote: 2.4 A note on tone. Ruruuli-Lunyala is a tonal language: tone is contrastive, i.e. it plays a role in distinguishing lexical items. A comprehensive study of the Ruruuli-Lunyala tone system is underway. The tone bearing unit is the mora (see also de Brito Gottlieb 2019). Preliminary findings suggest that Ruruuli-Lunyala has H, L and Ø tonal values whereby H and L are phonologically activated. Based on the three tone values, several surface tones are realised, they include: HL e.g. kifi [kífì] 'piece of meat (7)', falling contour LH͡LL, e.g. musale [mùsáàlè] 'tree (3)', downstep HH↓ H↓ HL, e.g. busigazi [óβú↓ sí↓ gázì] 'teenage years (14)', downdrift HHL↓ HL, e.g. ómúlà↑ múlì 'judge', and raised low HHH↑ L↓ HL tone ... The falling contour tone is realised on either a long vowel, e.g. [mùsáàlè] 'tree' or a vowel followed by a syllabic nasal, e.g. [kìbáǹja] 'untitled piece of land'.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place (sec. 2.4, p. 15 = PDF p. 31) in the held open-access LangSci volume. The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule stated' rests on the only grammar-level description of the language (2021, by the documentation project team). Web check (CrossRef/Semantic Scholar; 2020 Speech Prosody, fetched sources and read: it states explicitly 'There is no lexical stress' and shows lengthening is an intonation-phrase-final effect on both penult and final vowels, which confirms the coding and could be added as a second citation (optional refinement: prule could note 'no lexical stress (Zellers et al. 2020: 394); phrase-final penult+final lengthening is intonational'). sources.citation: Zellers, Margaret, Saudah Namyalo & Alena Witzlack-Makarevich. 2020. Investigating relationships between intonational and syntactic phrasing in Ruruuli/Lunyala. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2020, Tokyo, 394-398. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2020-81 (ISCA Archive, open).
sources.quote: p. 394: 'Ruruuli/Lunyala is a tone language, minimally involving a contrast between high and low tones, with the mora proposed as the tone-bearing unit [7]. ... There is no lexical stress, but it is possible that prominence marking may arise on a phrasal level.' p. 397: 'we find evidence for phrase-final lengthening in both the final and the penultimate syllable nuclei, affecting both short and long vowels' -- i.e. lengthening is an intonation-phrase boundary effect, not word stress.
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction, p. 394 (PDF p. 1), right column; discussion sec. 4, p. 397
sources.note: Only source that states the stress fact in so many words ('There is no lexical stress'); instrumental evidence that penultimate/final lengthening is phrasal. Our record's sketch is silent on stress, so this closes the argument-from-silence. fetched sources now.
